stem.text: Let \( f \) be a function with a continuous second derivative such that \( f(3) = 2 \), \( f'(3) = 2 \), and \( f''(3) = 1 \). Find the value of \( \lim_{x \to 3} \frac{f(x^{2} - 6) - 2}{\ln(x - 2)} \).

worked_solution.text: Because \( f \) is differentiable, it is continuous, so as \( x \to 3 \) the numerator \( f(x^{2} - 6) - 2 \) tends to 0, using \( f(3) = 2 \).
As \( x \to 3 \), the denominator \( \ln(x - 2) \) tends to \( 0 \).

The numerator and the denominator both tend to 0, so the form is \( \frac{0}{0} \) and L'Hospital's rule applies. Differentiate the numerator and the denominator separately: the limit equals \( \lim_{x \to 3} \frac{2x f'(x^{2} - 6)}{\frac{1}{x - 2}} \).
At \( x = 3 \) this numerator is \( 12 \) and this denominator is \( 1 \), which is not 0, so the limit is \( 12 \).
